items.stem: Define the term "digital public infrastructure (DPI)".
items.answer: Shared digital systems such as digital ID, payments and data exchange that enable public and private services, e.g. India's Aadhaar–UPI "India Stack"

items.stem: Distinguish between e-democracy and e-government.
items.answer: E-government uses technology to deliver services (tax filing, permits); e-democracy uses technology for citizen participation in decisions (e-voting, online consultations, petitions).
items.markingKey: E-government uses technology to deliver services (tax filing, permits); e-democracy uses technology for citizen participation in decisions (e-voting, online consultations, petitions). items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why digital technologies have become central to elections.
items.answer: Campaigns use data analytics and targeted social-media ads to reach voters, citizens get news through platforms, and electoral systems use digital registration and sometimes voting, creating both opportunities and risks (disinformation, hacking). (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.answer: A gig worker is paid per task through a platform and usually classified as self-employed, lacking guaranteed hours and benefits; an employee has a contract with rights such as minimum wage, sick pay and protection from unfair dismissal.

items.answer: AI can strengthen knowledge where it is transparent, verifiable and supports human sources; it weakens knowledge when it replaces them uncritically.

items.stem: Briefly explain why algorithmic management changes the balance of power between platforms and workers.
items.answer: Platforms control job allocation, pay rates, ratings and deactivation through opaque algorithms, while workers lack information and bargaining power, even though they are classified as independent.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Platforms control job allocation, pay rates, ratings and deactivation through opaque algorithms, while workers lack information and bargaining power, even though they are classified as independent. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Maya writes: "Smart technology always saves energy." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Devices, networks and data centres consume energy and resources; rebound effects (using more because it is efficient) can cancel savings.
items.markingKey: Devices, networks and data centres consume energy and resources; rebound effects (using more because it is efficient) can cancel savings. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between digital preservation and digital repatriation.
items.answer: Digital preservation creates and stores digital copies to protect heritage; digital repatriation returns digital copies (and control over them) to source communities.
items.markingKey: Digital preservation creates and stores digital copies to protect heritage; digital repatriation returns digital copies (and control over them) to source communities. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Online voting automatically increases turnout." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Evidence from Estonia and elsewhere shows modest effects on overall turnout; online voting also raises security and trust concerns.
items.markingKey: Evidence from Estonia and elsewhere shows modest effects on overall turnout; online voting also raises security and trust concerns. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the environmental costs of digital technology and the environmental benefits of digital technology.
items.answer: Benefits include efficiency and monitoring (smart grids, Global Forest Watch); costs include energy use by data centres, mining of minerals and e-waste.
items.markingKey: Benefits include efficiency and monitoring (smart grids, Global Forest Watch); costs include energy use by data centres, mining of minerals and e-waste. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which Masakhane and African-language NLP shows closing the language technology gap.
items.answer: Masakhane is a grassroots research community building natural-language-processing tools for African languages, created by African researchers. Community-led research challenges digital colonialism by building tools in and for under-served languages.
items.markingKey: Context (Masakhane is a grassroots research community building natural-language-processing tools for African languages, created by African researchers.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: community-led research challenges digital colonialism by building tools in and for under-served languages. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to closing the language technology gap.

items.stem: A party in a regional election spends US$2,000,000 on targeted social-media adverts at a cost of US$12 per 1,000 impressions. The click-through rate is 1.5%. Calculate the number of impressions and clicks. Explain one concern about micro-targeted political advertising.
items.answer: 166,666,667 impressions; 2,500,000 clicks; different voters see different, unaccountable messages (no shared public debate), and targeting may exploit personal data and vulnerabilities, as in the Cambridge Analytica case
items.markingKey: 2,000,000 ÷ 12 × 1000 = 166,666,667 impressions [M1 A1]; × 1.5% = 2,500,000 clicks [A1]. Concern: opacity/fragmentation of debate, use of personal data, manipulation, limited fact-checking [R1].

items.stem: A smartwatch feature alerts users to a possible heart-rhythm problem. Among 50,000 users, 3% have the condition. The feature detects 90% of real cases and wrongly alerts 2% of healthy users. Calculate the number of true alerts, false alerts and the percentage of alerts that are correct.
items.answer: 1,350 true, 970 false; 58.2% of alerts correct

items.stem: A heritage project must digitise 120,000 audio recordings of oral histories. A digitisation team can scan 1,000 items per working day, working 220 days a year. Calculate how many years digitisation will take. Explain one benefit and one risk of digitising cultural heritage.
items.answer: 0.5 years; benefit: preservation and global access; risk: loss of control by source communities, long-term digital preservation (file formats, storage) or commercial ownership

items.stem: With reference to Estonia's e-government (X-Road), explain how it illustrates political context: digital governance.
items.answer: Estonia connects public and private databases through the X-Road data-exchange layer; almost all public services are online and over half of votes in 2023 were cast online. Efficient digital government increases convenience and participation, but depends on high trust and strong cybersecurity.
items.markingKey: Context (Estonia connects public and private databases through the X-Road data-exchange layer; almost all public services are online and over half of votes in 2023 were cast online.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: efficient digital government increases convenience and participation, but depends on high trust and strong cybersecurity. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to political context: digital governance.

items.stem: Outline one way in which DeepMind and data-centre cooling shows technology addressing its own environmental footprint.
items.answer: Google used DeepMind machine learning to optimise cooling in its data centres, reporting up to 40% less cooling energy. AI improved efficiency, though overall data-centre energy demand has continued to grow with AI use.
items.markingKey: Context (Google used DeepMind machine learning to optimise cooling in its data centres, reporting up to 40% less cooling energy.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: AI improved efficiency, though overall data-centre energy demand has continued to grow with AI use. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to technology addressing its own environmental footprint.

items.stem: Using Wikipedia and ChatGPT as an example, explain AI and the human knowledge context.
items.answer: Wikipedia is a major source of training data for large language models, while AI-generated summaries may reduce visits to Wikipedia and its volunteer editing base. AI depends on a human knowledge commons it may also weaken, raising questions about the sustainability of shared knowledge.
items.markingKey: Context (Wikipedia is a major source of training data for large language models, while AI-generated summaries may reduce visits to Wikipedia and its volunteer editing base.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: AI depends on a human knowledge commons it may also weaken, raising questions about the sustainability of shared knowledge. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to AI and the human knowledge context.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Gig-economy platforms should be required to treat workers as employees."
items.answer: Platforms should give core protections (minimum pay, safety, transparency, appeal), as the EU Platform Work Directive aims, while allowing genuine flexibility.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: algorithmic control makes workers dependent (Uber v Aslam); employment rights reduce precarity. Arguments against: many workers value flexibility; platforms may raise prices or reduce work; a "third category" (workers) may balance both. Supported judgement: Platforms should give core protections (minimum pay, safety, transparency, appeal), as the EU Platform Work Directive aims, while allowing genuine flexibility.

items.stem: "Digital technology has improved health care more than any other area of life." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Digital health has brought major gains, but they are uneven and accompanied by new risks; comparisons with other contexts depend on criteria.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: telemedicine, wearables and AI diagnosis; pandemic tracking and vaccine research. Arguments against: data breaches and privacy risks; unequal access and over-diagnosis; other contexts (finance, communication) transformed as much. Supported judgement: Digital health has brought major gains, but they are uneven and accompanied by new risks; comparisons with other contexts depend on criteria. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: "Digital technology is the best way to preserve endangered cultures." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Digital tools are valuable when led by communities, but cannot replace intergenerational transmission and support for living cultures.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: recording languages, songs and stories; global access and education. Arguments against: culture lives in communities, not files; digital preservation needs funding and formats can become obsolete; consent and ownership concerns. Supported judgement: Digital tools are valuable when led by communities, but cannot replace intergenerational transmission and support for living cultures. Markbands (8 marks): Markbands (five bands, scaled to the marks available): top – focused on the question; accurate use of Digital Society concepts, content and contexts; specific, well-explained real-world examples; balanced analysis of impacts and implications for different stakeholders; a clear, well-supported conclusion. Upper-middle – relevant examples and some balance; conclusion reasoned. Middle – some relevant knowledge, partly descriptive; conclusion stated. Lower – limited, general knowledge, mainly descriptive. Bottom – minimal relevant material.
